summary: Defines a way for Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) routers to deal with equal-cost multipaths. Using hash algorithms to choose among the paths does not allow traffic to be spread well, so this document adds a redirect mechanism. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: If there are two equally good roads, you do not want all the trucks to pick the same one. This memo lets a router tell others which road to use so the load is shared.

questions: how does pim handle equal cost multipath
how does pim pick among equal cost paths
subtitle: How upstream PIM routers tell downstream routers which of several equal-cost links to join on.

tldr.problem: When several equal-cost paths lead upstream, each PIM router picks one on its own, for example by hashing. Operators cannot steer traffic across the paths by administrative metrics such as delay or path preference.
tldr.mechanism: An upstream router sends a PIM ECMP Redirect message on an interface it does not want used. The message names the preferred neighbor and carries a Preference and Metric that downstream routers use as tiebreakers.
tldr.outcome: Downstream routers can be told to share or split traffic across equal-cost links as the operator wants. RFC 6754 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 6754 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with Local Path Choice
sections.content:
A PIM router uses the Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) procedure to choose an upstream interface and a PIM neighbor on that interface. When there are equal-cost multipaths (ECMPs) upstream, existing implementations often use hash algorithms to pick one. The RFC gives two examples of such local choices: the neighbor with the highest IP address, or the neighbor with the best hash value over the destination and source addresses.

The weakness is that the choice is purely local. There is no straightforward way to tell two downstream routers to select either the same or different RPF neighbors for the same traffic flows. That usually leads to inefficient or ineffective use of network resources.

RFC 6754 introduces the ECMP Redirect. Upstream routers use a PIM ECMP Redirect message to instruct downstream routers how to tiebreak among the upstream neighbors, based on metrics chosen by the administrator, such as transmission delay, path preference or routing metrics.
sections.eli5: Each router used to pick a road by itself, so they often all picked the same one. Now the router at the other end can say which road to take.

sections.title: ECMP Bundles and Directions
sections.content:
In this RFC, ECMP means parallel, single-hop, equal-cost links between adjacent nodes. An ECMP bundle is a set of PIM-enabled interfaces on a router that all share the same routing metric. A router can have one or more bundles, an interface can belong to only one bundle, and bundles are created by configuration.

Upstream means towards the root of the multicast forwarding tree; an upstream router is one that is forwarding, or could forward, data onto interfaces in an ECMP bundle. Downstream means away from the root; a downstream router uses an interface in the bundle as its RPF interface for a forwarding entry.
sections.eli5: A bundle is a group of equally good roads between two towns. Upstream is toward the place the TV show comes from, and downstream is toward the people watching.

sections.title: How the Redirect Works
sections.content:
The design is modelled on the existing PIM Assert mechanism. Assert lets an upstream router notice several forwarders for the same flow on the same downstream interface, and carries a routing metric for tiebreaking. ECMP Redirect works in a similar way but resolves the choice among different interfaces in the ECMP.

The steps are:

  • A downstream router creates a new (*,G) or (S,G) entry, picks its RPF neighbor by the rules of RFC 4601 and sends its initial PIM Join there.
  • The upstream router sees that the Join arrived on an ECMP interface and checks whether the same flow is already going out of another ECMP interface.
  • If so, it sends a PIM ECMP Redirect onto the interface the Join came in on. The message holds the address of the desired RPF neighbor, an Interface ID (RFC 6395) and the tiebreaker parameters.
  • Downstream routers that receive it SHOULD trigger PIM Joins toward the new RPF neighbor.

Like Assert, the Redirect is sent by an upstream router, influences downstream RPF selection and uses a tiebreaker metric. The difference is that Assert selects an upstream router within one multi-access network such as a LAN, while Redirect selects both a network and an upstream router. Control messages are sent only when traffic needs to be rebalanced, which keeps control traffic down.
sections.eli5: When a router hears a request on the wrong road, it answers, "Use the other road, over here." It only speaks up when the load needs fixing.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Redirects
sections.content:
An upstream router sends ECMP Redirects in a rate-limited fashion when it detects a PIM Join, or multicast traffic, on a non-desired outgoing interface. An interface is non-desired when the router is already forwarding the same flow out of another interface in the same bundle, or when it is not yet forwarding the flow but another interface has more desired attributes. The router MAY skip Redirects if some downstream routers are unreachable over some links in the bundle.

The message points to the preferred interface using the Neighbor Address or the Interface ID. The Neighbor Address MUST belong to an interface in the same bundle as the interface the message goes out on. The Interface ID is used in IPv4 when some RPF neighbors are unnumbered, or in IPv6 where link-local addresses are in use; otherwise it is zeroed when sent and ignored on receipt. If it is not ignored, the receiver MUST use it instead of the Neighbor Address.

A downstream router that sees a different desired path from the one it uses should join the new path and prune the old one, in an implementation-specific order. If it receives Redirects from several upstream routers, it SHOULD use Preference, Metric and the other fields as tiebreakers, with the same procedure as PIM Assert in RFC 4601. An upstream router that receives a Redirect SHOULD NOT change its own forwarding behavior.

During a transient outage, such as a single cut link in a bundle, a downstream router SHOULD pick a new RPF neighbor, preferring one on the same LAN as the previous neighbor, and otherwise the router that served before the failure, identified by the Router ID inside the Interface ID.
sections.eli5: The router at the top only sends its "use the other road" note when someone is on the wrong road. Routers below read the notes and, if they get several, follow the one with the best score.

sections.title: Working with Routers That Do Not Support It
sections.content:
A PIM router that supports this specification MUST include the PIM ECMP Redirect Hello Option in its PIM Hello messages. A router sends Redirects on an interface only when all neighbors on that interface have sent the option. If any neighbor on a bundle lacks it, the router SHOULD NOT send Redirects on interfaces of that bundle, but SHOULD still process Redirects it receives there.

A router that does not support the specification simply ignores the Hello option and the Redirect messages in the PIM packets it receives.
sections.eli5: Routers first show each other a badge saying "I understand redirects." Notes are only sent when everyone on the road has a badge.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
The Hello option has Type 32 and Length 0, so it is only a flag. The Redirect message uses PIM message Type 11. Its PIM Version, Reserved and Checksum fields are as in Section 4.9 of RFC 4601.

After those come the Group Address (Encoded-Group format), the Source Address (Encoded-Unicast format), the Neighbor Address (32 or 128 bits) and a 64-bit Interface ID. The last two fields are the tiebreakers. Preference is 8 bits and is compared first, and a numerically smaller value is preferred. The reserved value 15 means that the Metric that follows is an NTP timestamp (RFC 5905), taken when the sender started forwarding out of that interface. Metric is 64 bits, compared second, again smaller wins, and can hold path parameters defined by users. If both are equal, the Neighbor Address or Interface ID is the third tiebreaker, whichever identifies the RPF neighbor, and the bigger value wins.
sections.eli5: The note has the show's name, who is sending it, which neighbor to use and two scores. The lowest score wins, and if scores tie the bigger address wins.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security of ECMP Redirect is only as good as the security of the PIM packet itself, and the considerations for PIM Assert packets in RFC 4601 apply. Spoofed Redirect packets may cause downstream routers to send PIM Joins to an undesired upstream router and trigger more Redirect messages. The considerations for PIM packets in RFC 4601 also apply to the new Hello option.
sections.eli5: A fake note could send routers down the wrong road, so the note is only as trustworthy as PIM itself.
